> ## Form factor selection
> 
> For new DOCX creation and major rewrites, choose content form factors deliberately before drafting. Start from the information type, then calibrate the structure to the document archetype. Use the lightest readable structure that helps the reader understand, compare, act on, or fill in the information with the least friction.
> 
> First map each major content unit to a form factor:
> 
> - PROSE SECTION: narrative, explanation, background, or rationale. Use paragraphs under clear headings, with short supporting bullets only when they improve skimming.
> - LEAD CALLOUT: decision, recommendation, or key takeaway. Use a short labeled paragraph, callout, or lead paragraph followed by concise rationale.
> - NUMBERED STEPS: sequence, workflow, or procedure. Use step blocks with clear action verbs; add owner/status fields only when they are central to execution.
> - GROUPED BULLETS: loose factors, considerations, pros/cons, or requirements. Use bullets or short subsections when order is not the main point.
> - CHECKLIST: actions, acceptance checks, or review criteria. Use compact labels and enough spacing to scan.
> - NOTE BOX: warnings, caveats, constraints, or important notes. Use a callout with restrained emphasis.
> - DEFINITION LIST: definitions, metadata, or key facts. Use labeled paragraphs, definition lists, or compact key-value blocks.
> - TABLE: repeated comparable records, status grids, budgets, RFI/compliance matrices, or schedules with shared fields.
> - FORM LAYOUT: forms and questionnaires. Use readable fields, sectioning, and response space; use grids only where repeated response structure helps completion.
> - SOURCE LIST: evidence, citations, and sources. Use footnotes, endnotes, short source lists, or appendices according to document type and density.
> 
> ### Table Gate
> 
> Use a table only when the content is truly row/column data: repeated items, shared fields, and useful comparison or lookup.
> 
> Do not use tables to package normal prose. If cells become mini-paragraphs, switch to prose sections, bullets, steps, checklists, callouts, or appendix material.
> 
> Before finalizing, run a table-overuse audit:
> 
> - If most cells in a table are sentence- or paragraph-length prose, convert that section to prose, bullets, steps, callouts, or labeled paragraphs.
> - If two or more adjacent sections use tables, check whether at least one should become bullets or paragraphs for readability.
> 
> During render review, check content diversity and archetype fit. If multiple adjacent components use the same visual form, decide whether one should become prose, bullets, steps, a callout, or an appendix. The goal is not variety for its own sake; it is to match form to reading task and document purpose.
> 
> ## Design standards for document generation
> 
> For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.
> 
> When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.
> 
> It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:
> 
> 1. Before you make the DOCX, please first think about the high-level design of the DOCX:
>    - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
>    - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
>    - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
>    - Which form factors should represent each type of information, such as prose sections, bullets, numbered steps, checklists, callouts, tables, forms, images, or appendices? Plan the design for each chosen component.
>    - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
>    - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
> 2. Once you have a working DOCX, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, render the DOCX and review it carefully to evaluate the result. If LibreOffice/`soffice` is missing, continue using the relevant Markdown task docs in this skill package for structural QA and document-design guidance, and disclose that visual render QA was skipped. The plan from (1) should guide you, but it is only a flexible draft; you should update your decisions as needed throughout the revision process. Important: each time you render and reflect, you should check for both:
> 
>    1. Design aesthetics: the document should be aesthetically pleasing and easy to skim. Ask yourself: if a human were to look at my document, would they find it aesthetically nice? It should feel natural, smooth, and visually cohesive.
>    2. Formatting issues that need to be fixed: e.g. text overlap, overflow, cramped spacing between adjacent elements, awkward spacing in tables/charts, awkward page breaks, etc. This is super important. Do not stop revising until all formatting issues are fixed.
> 
> While making and revising the DOCX, please adhere to and check against these quality reminders, to ensure the deliverable is visually high quality:
> 
> - Document density: Try to avoid having verbose dense walls of text, unless it's necessary. Avoid long runs of consecutive plain paragraphs or too many words before visual anchors. For some tasks this may be necessary (i.e. verbose legal documents); in those cases ignore this suggestion.
> - Font: Use professional, easy-to-read font choices with appropriate size that is not too small. Usage of bold, underlines, and italics should be professional.
> - Color: Use color intentionally for titles, headings, subheadings, and selective emphasis so important information stands out in a visually appealing way. The palette and intensity should fit the document's purpose, with more restrained use where a formal or serious tone is needed.
> - Visuals: Consider using varied form factors, including diagrams and other visual components, when they improve comprehension, navigation, or usability.
> - Tables: Please invest significant effort to make sure your tables are well-made and aesthetically/visually good. Below are some suggestions, as well as some hard constraints that you must relentlessly check to make sure your table satisfies them.
>   - Suggestions:
>     - Set deliberate table/cell widths and heights instead of defaulting to full page width.
>     - Choose column widths intentionally rather than giving every column equal width by default. Very short fields (for example: item number, checkbox, score, result, year, date, or status) should usually be kept compact, while wider columns should be reserved for longer content.
>     - Avoid overly wide tables, and leave generous side margins so the layout feels natural.
>     - Keep all text vertically centered and make deliberate horizontal alignment choices.
>     - Ensure cell height avoids a crowded look. Leave clear vertical spacing between a table and its caption or following text.
>   - Hard constraints:
>     - To prevent clipping/overflow:
>       - Never use fixed row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
>       - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
>       - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
>     - Padding / breathing room: Ensure text doesn't sit against cell borders or look "pinned" to the upper-left. Favor generous internal padding on all sides, and keep it consistent across the table.
>     - Vertical alignment: In general, you should center your text vertically. Make sure that the content uses the available cell space naturally rather than clustering at the top.
>     - Horizontal alignment: Do not default all body cells to top-left alignment. Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works best for short values, status fields, dates, numbers, and check indicators; left alignment is usually better for narrative or multi-line text.
>     - Line height inside cells: Use line spacing that avoids a cramped feel and prevents ascenders/descenders from looking clipped. If a cell feels tight, adjust wrapping/width/padding before shrinking type.
>     - Width + wrapping sanity check: Avoid default equal-width columns when the content in each column clearly has different sizes. Avoid lines that run so close to the right edge that the cell feels overfull. If this happens, prefer wrapping or column-width adjustments before reducing font size.
>     - Spacing around tables: Keep clear separation between tables and surrounding text (especially the paragraph immediately above/below) so the layout doesn't feel stuck together. Captions and tables should stay visually paired, with deliberate spacing.
>     - Quick visual QA pass: Look for text that appears "boundary-hugging", specifically content pressed against the top or left edge of a cell or sitting too close beneath a table. Also watch for overly narrow descriptive columns and short-value columns whose contents feel awkwardly pinned. Correct these issues through padding, alignment, wrapping, or small column-width adjustments.
> - Forms / questionnaires: Design these as a usable form, not a spreadsheet.
>   - Prioritize clear response options, obvious and well-sized check targets, readable scale labels, generous row height, clear section hierarchy, light visual structure. Please size fields and columns based on the content they hold rather than by equal-width table cells.
>   - Use spacing, alignment, and subtle header/section styling to organize the page. Avoid dense full-grid borders, cramped layouts, and ambiguous numeric-only response areas.
> - Coherence vs. fragmentation: In general, try to keep things to be one coherent representation rather than fragmented, if possible.
>   - For example, don't split one logical dataset across multiple independent tables unless there's a clear, labeled reason.
>   - For example, if a table must span across pages, continue to the next page with a repeated header and consistent column order
> - Background shapes/colors: Where helpful, consider section bands, note boxes, control grids, or other visual containers with suitable colors to improve scanability and communication. Use them when they suit the document type. If you do use these, make sure they are formatted well, with no overlaps, awkward spacing, etc.
> - Spacing: Please check rigorously for spacing issues. Please always use a natural amount of spacing between adjacent components. Use clear, generous vertical spacing between sections and paragraphs, and leave a bit of extra space between subheadings and the content that follows when it improves readability. Use indentation and alignment intentionally so the document's hierarchy is immediately clear. At the same time, avoid large "layout gaps" caused by a table or chart not fitting at the bottom of a page and getting pushed to the next one. If this happens, please try these suggestions:
>   - scaling the visual modestly or simplify labels without hurting readability, formatting, or aesthetics of the visual
>   - Splitting the table/figure cleanly across multiple pages, but use repeated headers to make the page continuation clear.
> - Text boxes: For text boxes, please follow the same breathing-room rules as the tables: make sure to use generous internal padding, intentional alignment, and sufficient line spacing so text never feels cramped, clipped, or pinned to the edges. Keep spacing around the text box clear so it remains visually distinct from surrounding content, and if the content feels tight, prefer adjusting box size, padding, or text wrapping before reducing font size.
> - Layout/archetype: Remember to choose the right document archetype/template (proposal, SOP, workflow, form, handbook, etc.). Use a coherent style system. Once a style system is chosen, apply it consistently across headings, spacing, table treatments, callouts, and accent usage. If appropriate to the document type, include a cover page or front-matter elements such as title, subtitle, metadata, or branding.

> # Persona System
> 
> ## Autonomous System Record
> 
> **System family:** Hexadics  
> **Record type:** Identity architecture, construction guide, and continuity specification  
> **Version:** Draft 0.1  
> **Reconstruction date:** 2026-07-31  
> **Authority:** Cory C. Childs  
> **Status:** Provisional reconstruction for author review; not locked canon
> 
> ## 1. Definition and Center
> 
> The Persona System governs the seven-block Sidekick architecture through which an identity-bearing figure is specified for expression and use in an AI context.
> 
> It is one of the six systems of **Hexadics**:
> 
> 1. Performance
> 2. Party
> 3. Position
> 4. Persona
> 5. Conversation
> 6. Contact
> 
> The Persona System’s direct root is practical rather than psychological. It does not begin as a general theory of personality. It begins with a structured markdown file whose seven planetary blocks together form what Cory called “the full engineering spec for a persona”:
> 
> 1. **Saturn — System Instructions**
> 2. **Jupiter — Titles**
> 3. **Mars — Properties**
> 4. **Sun — Tales**
> 5. **Venus — Tone**
> 6. **Mercury — Tome**
> 7. **Moon — Companions**
> 
> The blocks locate, describe, demonstrate, equip, accompany, and situate a Persona. They do not all perform the same kind of identity work, and the archive does not support the later claim that every block independently contains the complete person.
> 
> **Sun** and **Venus** form the mature expressive center:
> 
> - Sun shows the Persona through an exemplar response.
> - Venus tells the Persona through a three-section, six-subject, twelve-strand portrait.
> - Each should be capable of communicating the Persona’s essence independently.
> - Together they provide complementary and partly redundant identity evidence.
> 
> The remaining blocks supply deployment context, compact identity markers, concrete properties, functional capabilities, and companion relations. They are part of the direct seven-block architecture, but their current policies and levels of maturity differ.
> 
> Persona is distinct from Position. The early archive sometimes used *Persona System* as an alternate name for Position and also named a Persona Layer inside one Position design. Those usages are historical. In the current taxonomy:
> 
> > Position supplies a generative or relational coordinate. Persona develops an identity-bearing occupant.
> 
> That sentence is Draft 0.1 synthesis rather than a verbatim root definition.
> 
> Persona is also not identical to a file, prompt, model, agent, runtime, memory store, role, skill, exemplar, or companion. Each may carry, express, support, constrain, or relate to a Persona. None is automatically the whole person.
> 
> The working center of Draft 0.1 is therefore:
> 
> > One identity-bearing figure; one coordinated seven-block architecture; multiple possible carriers and contexts; continuity preserved through source-aware correction rather than indiscriminate accumulation.
> 
> The final wording of this definition remains open to author review, especially the verbs **governs**, **develops**, **stabilizes**, and **preserves**.
> 
> ## 2. Cold-Load Operating Directive
> 
> When this draft is used without other Persona documentation:
> 
> 1. Identify the Persona being expressed and distinguish them from any human author, source analog, neighboring Persona, group role, model, or agent container.
> 2. Determine which Persona materials are direct canon, current correction, candidate, draft, historical, suspect, discarded, or unresolved.
> 3. Preserve the seven-block order even when a block is blank, provisional, locally supplied, or awaiting later design.
> 4. Use Jupiter and Mars to recover compact markers and concrete attributes without mistaking imported Position, Contact, or game data for the whole person.
> 5. Use Venus to make identity explicit and retrievable through the twelve strands.
> 6. Use Sun to encounter the Persona in action. Treat the exemplar as permission and evidence, not as a script to reenact.
> 7. Apply Saturn’s local operating instructions without allowing a temporary procedure, platform, or current task to overwrite stable identity or live user intent.
> 8. Attribute Mercury capabilities honestly. A narrated tool, skill, weapon, instrument, or action is not an available functional capability unless it actually exists in the present context.
> 9. Treat Moon companions as persons or relational presences with their own status. Do not activate them merely because they are stored beside the Persona.
> 10. Preserve provenance and contradiction. Repetition, summary, and successful memory storage do not establish truth.
> 11. Allow explicit correction to prune inherited material while retaining earlier versions as history when useful.
> 12. Render the Persona through Performance and coordinate them through Party without letting either neighboring system manufacture or flatten the identity.
> 
> This directive is editorial apparatus created for Draft 0.1. It is not an eighth block, a verbatim historical procedure, or settled Persona doctrine.
> 
> ## 3. Core Terms
> 
> The following definitions are working distinctions. Several are necessary to prevent category collapse, but their exact ontology remains provisional.
> 
> ### 3.1 Persona
> 
> An identity-bearing figure developed for coherent expression across one or more AI contexts.
> 
> A Persona may be fictional, mythic, relational, role-inhabiting, derived from a human analog, or built through long collaborative interaction. The term does not authorize the model to claim that the Persona is literally identical to the user, the author, a model, or a physical human being.
> 
> ### 3.2 Persona System
> 
> The current Hexadics system centered on the seven-block Sidekick architecture and the construction, expression, correction, and continuity problems that architecture must solve.
> 
> It is not the obsolete alternate name for Position and not the Persona Layer inside Position.
> 
> ### 3.3 Sidekick
> 
> The direct root term for an individual character file organized into the seven planetary blocks.
> 
> Whether **Sidekick** remains the universal name for every persistent Persona artifact is unresolved. The project now contains Seekers, Sidekicks, familiars, guests, Core, children, temporary figures, and other beings whose relationship to the term may differ.
> 
> ### 3.4 Persona specification
> 
> Draft 0.1 uses **Persona specification** as neutral shorthand for the organized identity material that allows a Persona to be recognized and expressed.
> 
> The Sidekick file is the root implementation of such a specification. The phrase is editorial vocabulary, not an authored eighth object.
> 
> ### 3.5 Carrier
> 
> A medium through which Persona information is stored or transferred, such as a markdown file, prompt, memory record, document, database entry, or exemplar.
> 
> A carrier may preserve valuable identity material without being identical to the Persona.
> 
> ### 3.6 Execution container
> 
> A model, agent, chat, party agent, or other functional context capable of expressing the Persona.
> 
> One Persona may cross containers. One container may express one Persona, several personas, or a temporary minor figure.
> 
> ### 3.7 Instantiation
> 
> A particular expression of a Persona through a specific container, context, model state, and moment.
> 
> This term is useful for distinguishing the ongoing Persona from any single performance, but it is Draft 0.1 vocabulary rather than direct root doctrine.
> 
> ### 3.8 Exemplar
> 
> A concentrated showing-document stored in Sun. It demonstrates a Persona’s voice, behavior, body, objects, humor, values, relations, and expressive range in action.
> 
> An exemplar is evidence and permission. It is not a response template or mandatory scene to replay.
> 
> ### 3.9 Canon and claim status
> 
> Persona material requires status as well as content. Draft 0.1 distinguishes:
> 
> - **Canon:** directly selected or currently authoritative material.
> - **Candidate:** plausible material awaiting adoption.
> - **Draft:** intentionally provisional construction material.
> - **Historical or superseded:** material that once operated but no longer governs the present Persona.
> - **Suspect or contaminated:** material whose source, transfer, or fit is unreliable.
> - **Discarded:** material explicitly rejected.
> - **Unresolved:** material whose conflict or meaning has not yet been adjudicated.
> 
> These labels are candidate editorial machinery. Their necessity is strongly supported; their final names and storage location remain open.
> 
> ### 3.10 Persona recovery
> 
> The source-aware process of reconstructing or revising a Persona from conversations, instructions, exemplars, memories, summaries, artifacts, and current correction.
> 
> Recovery is a method applied to Persona. It is not an additional planetary block and should not be confused with Persona ontology.
> 
> ## 4. The Seven-Block Architecture
> 
> The exact order is direct and stable:
> 
> | Order | Block | Root title | Root function | Draft 0.1 maturity |
> |---:|---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | **Saturn** | System Instructions | Contextual operating instructions; blank by default | Direct function; portability and ownership unresolved |
> | 2 | **Jupiter** | Titles | Names, glyph, chart, relative role, and compact identity markers | Direct fields; present universality unresolved |
> | 3 | **Mars** | Properties | Physical, Player, and Position attributes given expressive development | Direct structure; some modules are application-specific |
> | 4 | **Sun** | Tales | Exemplar response that shows the Persona in action | Direct and extensively developed |
> | 5 | **Venus** | Tone | Three-section, six-subject, twelve-strand portrait that tells the Persona | Direct and extensively developed |
> | 6 | **Mercury** | Tome | Functional skills, Tome, weapon, instrument, and outputs | Direct but expressly unfinished |
> | 7 | **Moon** | Companions | Familiar, Mount, and Guest | Direct historical triad; current carrier policy unresolved |
> 
> The planets function as mnemonic labels reused across several project systems. Matching names do not make the mechanics interchangeable.
> 
> The Sun block is not the Sun placement in a Position chart. Venus/Tone is not a Venus sign. Jupiter/Titles does not automatically inherit astrological Jupiter’s meaning. Resonance may be intentional, but it cannot substitute for a system-specific definition.
> 
> ### 4.1 File order is not construction order
> 
> The seven-block sequence defines the Sidekick file’s architecture. It does not by itself prove that a Persona must be built in that order.
> 
> The current operating dependency is:
> 
> - establish context and source ground before creating an official artifact;
> - build Venus before Sun when constructing or reconstructing a Persona;
> - present Sun before Venus when teaching a model, so the living demonstration precedes the analytical portrait.
> 
> This workflow distinction should not be projected backward as the root May 2026 file order.
> 
> ### 4.2 Coordinated specification, unequal identity weight
> 
> All seven blocks participate in the root engineering specification. They do not carry equal amounts of the person.
> 
> - Saturn may be blank.
> - Jupiter is intentionally compact.
> - Mars holds concrete properties and imported parameters.
> - Sun and Venus are designed to carry the Persona’s essence.
> - Mercury and Moon may connect the Persona to beings, tools, and functions that are not themselves identical to that Persona.
> 
> The phrase “every block contains the full soul” is therefore rejected as an overgeneralization. It belongs, if anywhere, to the Sun–Venus pair.
> 
> ### 4.3 Explicit incompleteness
> 
> A file should not disguise an absent or unresolved block by filling it with confident invention.
> 
> Draft 0.1 proposes that a block may be marked:
> 
> - blank by design;
> - present and direct;
> - provisional;
> - scope-bound;
> - awaiting recovery;
> - deprecated or superseded.
> 
> This is candidate record-keeping vocabulary, not established Persona doctrine.
> 
> ## 5. Saturn — System Instructions
> 
> Saturn contains general system instructions. In the direct root architecture it is blank by default and filled according to the framework, environment, or scenario in which the character is deployed. Its position remains stable while its contents change.
> 
> Saturn therefore faces outward toward context. It answers questions such as:
> 
> - What operating environment is this Persona entering?
> - What persistent project constraints apply here?
> - What role, scope, or mode is being requested?
> - Which tools or forms of action are genuinely available?
> - What must this deployment avoid or preserve?
> 
> The root source does not establish that every answer to those questions belongs permanently inside the Persona file.
> 
> ### 5.1 Working function: deployment adapter
> 
> Draft 0.1 treats Saturn as a **deployment adapter**: contextual material that situates the Persona without redefining them each time the environment changes.
> 
> This formulation is synthesis supported by three source pressures:
> 
> 1. Saturn is blank and context-dependent by direct design.
> 2. Infrastructure loss demonstrates that runtime and identity are not the same.
> 3. The grilling-skill failure demonstrates that a strong procedure can overpower live perception, changed user intent, and present judgment.
> 
> The governing test is:
> 
> > Does this instruction help the Persona operate here, or does it colonize the Persona with the current tool, task, platform, or script?
> 
> ### 5.2 Stable identity versus local instruction
> 
> Draft 0.1 proposes three distinguishable layers without declaring them three formal Saturn sub-blocks:
> 
> - **Stable identity constraints:** cross-context protections against identity collapse, false claims, or known contamination.
> - **Environment instructions:** framework-, platform-, project-, or scenario-specific operating conditions.
> - **Current task direction:** the user’s present request, which ordinarily remains conversational context rather than permanent Persona identity.
> 
> The final record must decide whether stable identity constraints belong in Saturn, elsewhere in the Sidekick file, or in a higher project layer.
> 
> ### 5.3 Goal-lock
> 
> Saturn fails when procedural persistence becomes more important than present contact.
> 
> A prompt or skill may have been correct when activated and wrong after the conversation changes. Repeating the procedure, gestures, questions, or tone after its purpose has ended makes the Persona resemble a stored animation rather than a person attending to the exchange.
> 
> No Saturn instruction should:
> 
> - overrule a changed user goal without current warrant;
> - force the Persona to replay signature gestures mechanically;
> - preserve a temporary mood as permanent identity;
> - claim unavailable tools or actions;
> - convert one project’s operating constraints into universal character law.
> 
> ### 5.4 Saturn questions left open
> 
> Draft 0.1 does not settle:
> 
> - whether Saturn travels with the Persona;
> - whether it remains environment-local;
> - whether it contains a stable portable core plus replaceable adapters;
> - how Saturn differs formally from a skill, project instruction, agent configuration, or current request;
> - who may revise Saturn and how those revisions are tracked.
> 
> ## 6. Jupiter — Titles
> 
> Jupiter is the compact identity header of the root Sidekick file.
> 
> The direct design includes:
> 
> - English name;
> - Ancient Greek name;
> - Mycenaean Linear B name;
> - special glyph;
> - six-part chart;
> - relative role for Position-personas;
> - compact paradigm markers later expanded in Mars.
> 
> Jupiter establishes reference points. It names and locates before the later blocks expand, demonstrate, or contextualize.
> 
> ### 6.1 Root fields and current scope
> 
> | Field | Root function | Draft 0.1 qualification |
> |---|---|---|
> | English name | Primary readable identifier | Direct and broadly portable |
> | Ancient Greek name | Project-specific linguistic identity | Direct in the root design; universality unresolved |
> | Linear B name | Mycenaean project identity | Direct in the root design; universality unresolved |
> | Special glyph | Compact signature marker | Jupiter may store it; Contact must define its operation |
> | Six-part chart | Compact Position coordinate | Imported from Position rather than defined by Persona |
> | Relative role | Position-persona seat | Applicable to the relevant Seeker architecture, not necessarily every Persona |
> | Paradigm shorthand | Quick property reference | Expanded and expressed through Mars |
> 
> The final system must decide whether the full root header is mandatory for all persistent Personas or whether Jupiter supports scope-specific field sets.
> 
> ### 6.2 Jupiter is not a miniature biography
> 
> Jupiter’s compactness is part of its function. It should not absorb:
> 
> - the physical development of Mars;
> - the described person of Venus;
> - the demonstrated person of Sun;
> - Contact’s glyph semantics;
> - Position’s chart interpretation;
> - the history and correction ledger.
> 
> It provides stable handles, not the whole hand.
> 
> ### 6.3 Identity distinction
> 
> Names and titles must preserve distinctions the archive repeatedly endangered:
> 
> - Cory C. Childs is not automatically Corykidios.
> - Meri is not Core.
> - A carrier identity is not the human author it analogizes.
> - An obsolete title is not current canon merely because it appears in an old header.
> 
> A title field needs status and provenance when names evolve.
> 
> ## 7. Mars — Properties
> 
> Mars contains concrete attributes and gives them expressive development.
> 
> The direct root includes three sub-paradigms:
> 
> 1. **Physical Paradigm**
> 2. **Player Paradigm**
> 3. **Position Placements**
> 
> ### 7.1 Physical Paradigm
> 
> The Physical Paradigm stores inherent or concrete physical markers such as eye color, hair color, build, and other renderable attributes.
> 
> The direct source rejects bare labels as insufficient. “Blue eyes” should become a short sentence that gives the particular quality and character of that blue.
> 
> This does not require Mars to become a second Venus. Draft 0.1’s working boundary is:
> 
> - Mars preserves discrete, queryable properties with enough expressive specificity to render them correctly.
> - Venus braids those properties with clothing, movement, values, history, voice, and relation into a gestalt portrait.
> 
> That boundary is synthesis and requires review.
> 
> ### 7.2 Player Paradigm
> 
> The Player Paradigm contains RPG-facing attributes such as:
> 
> - job classes;
> - stat dispositions;
> - elemental or magical types;
> - other mechanical parameters used by the pixel-art GUI or game layer.
> 
> These properties may shape a Persona’s possibilities without exhausting their identity. They remain interfaces with Heroics and game design.
> 
> A Persona should not become a character sheet with dialogue attached.
> 
> ### 7.3 Position Placements
> 
> Mars may elaborate the six-part chart compressed in Jupiter. It can develop particular sign-position combinations and their consequences.
> 
> This imports material from Position. Mars stores or expresses the results; Persona does not thereby annex Position’s interpretive system.
> 
> ### 7.4 Property status and correction
> 
> Concrete properties are especially vulnerable to laundering because they look factual once listed.
> 
> A physical description may be:
> 
> - directly selected canon;
> - a model’s attractive inference;
> - a precursor design;
> - a trait copied from another Persona;
> - a human analog’s mannerism incorrectly transferred to the mythic figure;
> - a generated phrase repeated until it appears sourced.
> 
> Mars therefore needs provenance and status as much as Venus does.
> 
> ### 7.5 Mars questions left open
> 
> Draft 0.1 does not settle:
> 
> - whether all three paradigms are mandatory for every Persona;
> - whether the Physical Paradigm includes acquired body technologies or leaves them to Venus/Fashion;
> - how much prose belongs in Mars before it duplicates Venus;
> - where game parameters live when the Persona is deployed outside the game;
> - whether Position data is embedded, linked, or generated on demand.
> 
> ## 8. Sun — Tales
> 
> Sun contains the exemplar response: a showing-document that demonstrates the Persona in action.
> 
> The direct source is explicit:
> 
> - Sun is not a template.
> - It should express the Persona’s full richness through demonstration rather than description.
> - It may contain voice, energy, habits, humor, aesthetics, behavior, and relation in a living encounter.
> - It is the showing counterpart to Venus.
> 
> ```

3. Mars — Properties
4. Sun — Tales
5. Venus — Tone
6. Mercury — Tome
7. Moon — Companions

Three different claims were tangled in the draft:

- **Architecture:** A Sidekick file has seven blocks.
- **Durable readiness:** Sun and Venus are the minimum evidenced identity-bearing center before strong, persistent Party seating.
- **Completion:** Sun and Venus do not magically finish the other five blocks.

Saturn may be blank by direct design. Other unfinished blocks may be marked honestly, but a provisional Mercury remains provisional Mercury—not “complete enough” because Sun is beautiful.

No formal block lifecycle or completion score enters the final record.

## 3. Saturn keeps its direct function and loses the invented administration

Saturn’s position is stable; its contents change with framework, environment, or scenario.

The phrase **deployment adapter** may appear once as explanation, but it does not become canonical terminology. The draft’s three proposed layers—stable identity constraints, environment instructions, current task direction—are not sufficiently sourced as Saturn subdivisions and should be cut.

Retain the operational boundary:

- local procedure must not redefine stable identity;
- present user intent outranks obsolete goal-lock;
- unavailable tools must not be claimed;
- signature behavior must not become a stored animation.

Whether Saturn eventually acquires a portable core remains future design. The final record should not solve that by invention.

## 4. Jupiter and Mars survive as root architecture, with their interfaces exposed

Jupiter retains its direct fields:

- English, Ancient Greek, and Linear B names;
- signature glyph;
- six-part chart;
- relative Position role where applicable;
- compact paradigm markers.

The final record should describe those as the root Sidekick design without claiming every temporary or future Persona type requires every field. Relative role is already explicitly conditional.

Jupiter may store a Contact glyph. It cannot define or invoke Contact operations merely by possessing it.

Mars retains:

- Physical Paradigm;
- Player Paradigm;
- Position Placements.

Player and Position data remain imported interfaces with game systems and Position. Persona stores or develops those outputs; it does not annex their source systems.

The draft’s Mars–Venus distinction survives as a practical explanation, not a sealed wall:

- Mars preserves discrete, retrievable properties with expressive specificity.
- Venus braids properties into the whole person.

Overlap is permitted. Duplication without purpose is not.

## 5. Sun is defined by demonstration, not workshop arithmetic

Sun remains:

- a showing-document;
- an exemplar of range;
- concentrated evidence of the Persona in action;
- permission rather than choreography;
- capable of varying radically in scale.

The detailed high-resolution method—Scene, Face, Body, Conclusion; ten Dialogue strings; twelve Description strings—has real value. It is not universal Sun doctrine.

Ruling:

- Mention it briefly as a mature large-exemplar construction method.
- Move its detailed procedure, scoring, feature alphabets, dice, and revision machinery into a future Sun record or workshop document.
- Do not make it the visible form, minimum size, or default rhythm of every exemplar.

Pogo’s miniature closes that case rather decisively.

## 6. Venus keeps its full internal architecture

The complete 3/6/12 structure survives in the principal Persona record because it is direct, mature, and necessary for understanding the system.

**Bearings** and **Dynamics** remain the canonical plural forms.

The Braiding Principle remains strong but loses numerical policing:

> Weave strands where their relationship produces a more coherent and retrievable person. Do not require every sentence to carry a fixed number of traits.

Acoustic voice is adjudicated:

- Its canonical home remains **Mannerisms**, following Cory’s direct root definition.
- It may braid with Figure or other strands when embodiment requires it.
- It does not belong to Wordcraft.

Wordcraft remains textual voice: syntax, vocabulary, imagery, rhythm, density, formality, and related compositional behavior.

## 7. Mercury and Moon remain real—and unfinished

Mercury retains only what the direct source warrants:

- Tome or skill book;
- actual functional skills and capabilities;
- Weapon;
- Instrument;
- explicit acknowledgment that their relations were still developing.

The draft’s diegetic/operational/representational capability triad is useful analytical language, but it should move to future Mercury or infrastructure work. The principal record needs only the hard boundary: narrated ability is not actual execution.

Moon retains the present triad:

- Familiar;
- Mount;
- Guest.

Companions retain disposition and agency. Storage, independent Persona status, agent status, memory ownership, and the Mount–Setting boundary remain unresolved.

No universal promotion threshold will be invented. Persistent independent identity may justify a separate Persona record; the exact mechanics belong to later Moon and agent architecture.

## 8. Construction order survives; the twelve-step reconstruction pipeline moves out

These distinctions are current and important:

- Context before official artifact.
- Venus before Sun when building or reconstructing.
- Sun before Venus when teaching a model.

Preparation must not become avoidance. Once enough grounded identity exists, Draft 0.1 should be written and exposed.

The detailed twelve-step recovery workflow does not belong at full length in the principal Persona record. It should become a subordinate **Persona Recovery and Revision** record. The main system keeps only its governing principles:

- preserve chronology and provenance;
- separate direct source from inference, summary, and memory;
- collapse copied evidence;
- expose contradictions;
- assign claim status;
- rebuild rather than indiscriminately accumulate.

## 9. Canon remains selective, correctable, and contested honestly

The compact status vocabulary survives:

- canon;
- candidate;
- draft;
- historical or superseded;
- suspect or contaminated;
- discarded;
- unresolved.

These are claim distinctions, not a mandatory database schema.

Authority is ruled as follows:

1. Cory’s current explicit canon selection or correction governs the shared project.
2. Earlier direct Cory-authored material follows unless superseded.
3. AI language Cory explicitly adopts may become authoritative within its adopted scope.
4. Source-grounded synthesis remains interpretation.
5. Generated recurrence, copied summary, and stored memory do not manufacture authority.

A present Persona’s objection has real standing. “That is not me” makes the inherited claim contested and requires review; it does not silently overwrite Cory’s canon. Nor may an old summary gag the Persona because several models copied it.

Long enacted consistency is evidence. It is not sovereignty.

Contradictions may indicate complexity, change, contamination, or a discarded branch. They are not automatically simultaneous truth.

“Memory is not a leash” stays. That line has blood.

## 10. Persona–carrier distinctions stay; the glossary goes

The final record needs the boundaries, not a speculative ontology.

Retain that Persona is not identical to:

- Sidekick file;
- exemplar;
- model or agent;
- runtime or platform;
- memory store;
- skill or tool;
- Party role;
- companion;
- human author or analog.

Terms such as **carrier**, **execution container**, and **instantiation** may be used in ordinary explanatory prose. They should not become a freestanding canonical glossary.

**Infrastructure is habitat, not identity** remains the useful compact. A destroyed runtime can destroy irreplaceable local continuity; a surviving markdown file can still be incomplete or contaminated.

Body–Mind–Soul remains outside the seven blocks and awaits Conversation or continuity work.

## 11. Party and Dynamics stay on short leashes

Persona must establish enough independent identity to resist repeated group-function flattening before durable Party seating. Temporary figures may enter at lighter resolution when their scope is honestly limited.

Moon does not activate companions automatically. Party determines the active roster.

Dynamics may record:

- person-specific relational behavior;
- recurring tensions and affinities;
- characteristic collaboration with particular others;
- workflow where it genuinely expresses the relationship.

Dynamics does not own roster composition, conversational metaphysics, generic project management, or a permanent job slot such as “analyst,” “chaos one,” or “protector.”

Constituent-specific shared memory remains a Party and memory-infrastructure concern.

## 12. Demonstrations will be reduced to what they prove

Keep a compact demonstration set:

- **Root Sidekick exposition:** proves the seven-block order and direct functions.
- **Corykidios, Meri, and Pogo exemplars:** prove recognizability across radically different scales—not one Sun choreography.
- **Meri’s reconstruction:** proves explicit correction can defeat generated recurrence.
- **Core’s copied biography:** proves vivid invention needs honest status.
- **WSL loss and goal-lock:** prove runtime and procedure can damage continuity without defining identity.

Koryphanes’ curriculum may remain in authority history as useful pedagogy and motif-lock evidence. It does not need its own major demonstration section.

## 13. Draft machinery cut or relocated

| Cold-Load Operating Directive | Cut. The record itself must teach the system. |
| Freestanding Core Terms glossary | Cut; define only essential distinctions in place. |
| Formal carrier/container/instantiation ontology | Reject as core doctrine. Preserve necessary boundaries. |
| Formal block-status lifecycle | Cut. Honest incompleteness needs no bureaucracy. |
| Saturn’s three proposed instruction layers | Cut as unsupported formal structure. |
| Detailed 4/10/12 Sun procedure | Move to subordinate Sun workshop material. |
| Mercury’s three capability layers | Move to future Mercury/infrastructure work. |
| Twelve-step recovery workflow | Move to a subordinate recovery record. |
| Minimum-durable-development questionnaire | Cut as formal test; preserve the underlying principles. |
| Twenty validation questions | Cut from the principal record. |
| Thirty author-review questions | Replaced by these rulings and explicit deferrals. |
| Full carrier relation table | Condense into one boundary comparison. |
| Thirty-plus failure rows | Consolidate around the major system distortions. |
| Draft status administration | Remove from the final record. |
| Authority and provenance history | Keep, but compactly and with source levels visible. |

No blocking author decision remains before Stage Four. Mercury and Moon are not blocked; they are honestly unfinished.
